references.text: Jesus' teaching in the Sermon on the Mount about loving your enemies and being children of the heavenly Father, who causes his sun to rise on the evil and the good – a direct parallel to Luke 6:35.
Jesus asks what reward one gets if one only loves those who love you back – the same principle of going beyond the ordinary as in Luke 6:35.
The command from the Mosaic Law to love your neighbor as yourself, which Jesus expands to also include enemies in Luke 6:35.
Whoever shows mercy to the poor lends to the Lord – connected to the exhortation in Luke 6:35 to lend without expecting anything back.
If your enemy is hungry, give him food – an Old Testament principle of doing good to enemies, which is at the heart of Luke 6:35.
Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God – a parallel to the promise in Luke 6:35 that they will be children of the Most High.
Paul quotes the principle of giving food and drink to your enemy and overcoming evil with good, in line with Jesus' command to love enemies in Luke 6:35.
The righteous shows mercy and lends – connected to the exhortation in Luke 6:35 to lend without expecting anything back.
It goes well for those who show mercy and lend – a parallel to lending without expecting repayment in Luke 6:35.
The immediate context where Jesus commands to love enemies, do good to those who hate you, and bless those who curse you – the very foundation that is expanded in verse 35.
The Lord is called the Most High (Eljon) – background for the title 'children of the Most High' used in Luke 6:35.
Jesus is called the Son of the Most High – an expression that echoes in Luke 6:35 where believers are also called children of the Most High.
Paul urges to be good and merciful, and to forgive one another – this reflects the goodness that characterizes God's children in Luke 6:35.
A great reward awaits in heaven for those who are persecuted – a parallel to the promise of great reward in Luke 6:35.
God is love, and we should love each other because God loved us first – an elaboration on the divine example of love that underlies Luke 6:35.
